strengths: Addresses an important evaluation problem for brain-to-text NLP: fluent generation may not demonstrate generalization to unfamiliar subjects or stimuli. Auditing this distinction is a worthwhile contribution without requiring a new decoding architecture.

The taxonomy usefully distinguishes subject overlap, repeated stimuli, and overlapping fMRI windows. Experiments cover Narratives and ZuCo, two decoding systems, and four seeds for overlap measurements. The substantial reported differences across splits motivate closer scrutiny of evaluation practices.

Jointly holding out subjects and stimuli is appropriate for the stated generalization target. The manuscript considers modality-specific sampling differences, provides some implementation details, and acknowledges that its approach discards data.
weaknesses: The central causal claims are not established (§4.4). Decreasing reconstruction validation loss does not demonstrate encoder degradation, and improving test scores over training does not prove memorization. The randomly initialized encoder still receives real signals and training; its comparison also changes learning rate and training duration. Text-only and shuffled/noise-signal controls with matched optimization are needed to support the claim that generation ignores cognitive signals.

The contamination framing conflates different evaluation targets. Sharing subjects across independent recordings can be legitimate when decoding new text for a calibrated subject. Joint subject/stimulus holdout introduces distribution shifts, so lower performance alone does not establish that earlier evaluations were invalid. The conclusions should distinguish actual sample leakage from protocols that evaluate a different generalization setting.

The split pseudocode does not enforce its guarantee as written. Algorithm 1, line 15 checks subject membership but does not exclude stimuli assigned to validation/test; Algorithm 2, line 33 checks task membership but does not exclude held-out subjects. The edge-extension step can therefore reintroduce prohibited overlap. Loop/index definitions also conflict with the construction described in §3.3. Correct pseudocode and explicit verification of pairwise disjointness are necessary.

The leakage definitions and reported metrics require clarification. Equation 7 uses exact signal intersections to quantify subject overlap and leaves a zero denominator for entirely unseen subjects, making Table 1 difficult to reproduce. Table 3 reports ROUGE-1 F=84.64 with P=63.16 and R=71.50 for UniCoRN at 80 epochs under split (c), which is incompatible with standard F1 under consistent aggregation. This may be a transcription error, but the scoring needs verification.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the claimed benchmark release. The manuscript supplies no code or split-download link, actual partition assignments, or retained/discarded sample counts. Evaluation procedures also need to specify free-running generation versus ground-truth prefixes or teacher forcing. These details directly affect whether the benchmark measures genuine decoding.

The four-seed analysis covers overlap rates only; generation results lack variability across splits or training runs. Moreover, changing the partition also changes training-data availability and test composition, without controls separating these effects from overlap removal. This is particularly consequential with only 12 ZuCo participants. These addressable soundness and reproducibility gaps warrant resubmission next cycle before a Findings recommendation.
